hook: Before you even reach the description, SCP-106's file shows its containment procedures being rewritten, and failing. Treat the revision notes as part of the story. They tell you more about the threat than any adjective could.
whyItMatters:
The Old Man is one of the classic Keter-class pursuers, and his ability to sink into solid surfaces and drag victims into a private pocket dimension is an idea many later entities echo. He is also one of the most recognizable figures from SCP - Containment Breach, which brought him to a wide audience.

The article is credited to Dr Gears, whose name is also on SCP-914 and, with a co-author, SCP-682. Reading the three together is a good way to see how one early writer moved between clinical horror, menace and dry curiosity.
thingsToNotice:
The stacked revisions are a clever device: each superseded version is stamped as discontinued with a reason, so you watch the Foundation learn by failing. The final version's odd specifics, such as layered walls, random supports and sudden floodlights, read as lessons paid for in earlier breaches.

Notice the warning that 106 has no docile state and that quiet periods should be treated as a lure. That inversion, calm meaning danger, is the article's core fear. The recovery procedure at the end is deliberately uncomfortable, showing that the Foundation's solution carries a moral cost, stated in exactly the same flat procedural voice as everything else.

related.note: Another Keter whose file is shaped by a history of repeated breaches.
A different impossible space that you should never follow anything into.
